content: Early dietary intake may play a role in the development of allergic diseases. It is important to investigate whether supplementation with polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) or their addition to infant formula can prevent the onset of allergies. The objective of this study was to evaluate whether a higher intake of PUFAs during infancy could reduce the risk of developing allergic diseases. A comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL databases up to September 14, 2015. Additional searches included clinical trial registries, conference proceedings, and reference lists of relevant articles. The focus was on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized trials comparing PUFA supplementation with no supplementation in infants for allergy prevention. Two independent reviewers selected studies, assessed their quality, and extracted data. Fixed-effect analyses were used, and treatment effects were expressed as risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). The GRADE approach was applied to evaluate the quality of evidence. Seventeen studies were identified that examined the effects of higher versus lower PUFA intake on allergic outcomes in infants. However, only nine studies involving 2,704 infants provided data suitable for meta-analysis. Eight of these studies raised methodological concerns. In infants up to two years of age, meta-analyses showed no significant differences in the incidence of overall allergies (1 study, 323 infants; RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.26), asthma (3 studies, 1,162 infants; RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.35), dermatitis/eczema (7 studies, 1,906 infants; RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.06), or food allergies (3 studies, 915 infants; RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.19). However, there was a reduction in allergic rhinitis (2 studies, 594 infants; RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.96), with a number needed to treat for benefit (NNTB) of 25. In children aged two to five years, meta-analyses found no significant differences in the incidence of overall allergic diseases (2 studies, 154 infants; RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.02), asthma (1 study, 89 infants; RR 0.45, 95% CI 0.20 to 1.02), dermatitis/eczema (2 studies, 154 infants; RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.34 to 1.24), or food allergies (1 study, 65 infants; RR 2.27, 95% CI 0.25 to 20.68). In children aged two to five years, no significant differences were observed in the prevalence of overall allergic diseases (2 studies, 633 infants; RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.19), asthma (2 studies, 635 infants; RR 1.12, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.53), dermatitis/eczema (2 studies, 635 infants; RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.09), allergic rhinitis (2 studies, 635 infants; RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.25), or food allergies (1 study, 119 infants; RR 0.27, 95% CI 0.06 to 1.19). The authors concluded that there is no evidence to support that PUFA supplementation during infancy reduces the risk of allergies, asthma, dermatitis/eczema, or food allergies in infants or children. The quality of evidence was very low, and there was insufficient data to determine the effect on allergic rhinitis.
